speechtext:
I thank the House for allowing me to conclude my observations. I would have many other things to say on this subject, but others will have the opportunity to express their views. I would like to end with the motion moved by the mover, this afternoon, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe, asking that a royal commission be instituted to find out the causes of organized crime.
Mr. Speaker, I do not know if the member for Saint-Hyacinthe is serious about it. I hope he is. I know he has wide experience in this field since he has been a lawyer, a judge, a minister, and a judge again. I think he is one of those who best know the problems of organized crime, not only from the criminal's, but also from the victim's point of view.
For years, we have had royal commissions in Quebec, and in Canada too, not particularly on organized crime, but on other problems. Two kinds of inquiries are now being conducted in Quebec, one on crime in general and the other on the problems of building trades which, strangely enough, have some similitude with organized crime.
Several years ago, an inquiry was conducted by Mayor Drapeau of Montreal in cooperation with Mr. Pacifique Plante. What was the net result? Not very much! Another inquiry was launched a couple of years ago, I believe. What further result did it produce? Nothing much! We now have yet another inquiry. We find that crime exists, it is obvious, but what is being done against the criminal?
We have often seen hardened criminals apprehended after committing a loathsome crime. Police officers have risked their life to apprehend these criminals, the latter are put in prison and a few days later, they are back on the streets, as free men, making faces at the police officers that had arrested them.
One wonders if it is worthwhile risking the life of police officers to arrest loathsome individuals when it is known that a few days later they will be as free as wind and will continue committing more crimes. It is well known that some individuals are now free after buying their evasion way out and they are endangering everyone's life.
Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier and as others have pointed out, I think that we should pay more attention to criminals than to crimes.
November 12, 1974

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE GOVERNMENT ACTION TO COMBAT ORGANIZED CRIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I want to assure the House that, with the opposition, the government is most concerned about the growth of crime and criminal conspiracies in Canada. We would agree with the motion, that there are particular problems with respect to the drug trade in British Columbia, loan sharking in Ontario and mafia-type conspiracies in Quebec. The government has increased, and continues to increase, its activities to combat crime through the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and by other means to protect the public and to bring these criminals to justice. I will speak first about the increasingly serious problem of abuse and trafficking in illicit drugs which, as hon. members have pointed out, continues to escalate in most communities in Canada. It is clear to all of us that the trafficking in and use of heroin, cocaine and the abuse of chemicals such as methamphetamine-Speed-MDA, LSD and other related drugs is a problem of increasing dimensions and a major cause for concern.
The use of heroin by the younger generation is on the rise. As recently as 1968 there were only 12 known habitual users of heroin in Canada under the age of 20. In 1973, this total had increased to 709. It is estimated today there are between 16,000 and 19,000 heroin addicts in Canada. It is also significant to note that Europe used to be the major source of supply for heroin entering Canada. During the past year, however, all indications are that most of the heroin entering Canada originated in Southeast Asia. The European supply was cut back due to rigorous enforcement in France and lack of heroin cultivation in Turkey. As many members know, the Turkish government has reversed its stand and will again allow cultivation of heroin.
With respect to cannabis, a significant development is the recent interest in importation and trafficking of cannabis drugs on the part of major criminal organizations. In the recent past, those primarily involved with the importation and trafficking of cannabis were the younger entrepreneurs. During 1973, five gangland-style murders in Montreal were directly connected to an investigation on the importation of hashish.
The Royal Canadian Mountain Police presently assumes primary responsibility for investigating offences of trafficking in drugs at all levels of police jurisdiction, local, provincial, interprovincial and international. Drug trafficking is a large, highly organized criminal operation involving contacts and resources at all levels of jurisdiction. Competent drug law enforcement requires a comprehensive and consistent process in the total community. Specialists in drug law enforcement are capable of dealing with specific situations, as is presently the practice of members of the RCMP special drug squads, but consistent enforcement at an adequate level will only be accomplished efficiently by all police forces and all members of those police forces assuming responsibility for enforcement.
As far as the federal government and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are concerned, the following priorities for drug law enforcement are required: (a) the RCMP to provide leadership to improve drug intelligence, co-ordination and co-operation between all police department;
Organized Crime
(b) the RCMP to have primary responsibility for enforcement of drug trafficking offences at international, national, provincial and local levels and to provide assistance as required to other police forces where resources are available; (c) as a general rule, all police forces should accept responsibility for drug law enforcement within their respective jurisdictions and should be encouraged to develop the capacity for drug law enforcement where it is now lacking.
The RCMP offers a two-week drug investigation course for members of municipal and provincial police departments. In 1972-73, 38 members of municipal and provincial police departments took advantage of this course. In 197475, 123 members attended these courses. Hon. members should also note that the number of federal drug enforcement positions in the RCMP has increased from 102 in 1969-70 to 543 projected for 1975-76. For the fiscal year 1973-74, in excess of one million man-hours was expended by the RCMP in drug law enforcement.
I should also point out that because of the increase in the scope and size of international and national traffic in illicit narcotics, the drug enforcement program now includes international investigations. Many successful international investigations have been conducted by the RCMP in France, Italy, The Netherlands, England, Spain, Lebanon, Pakistan, India, Hong Kong mainland, Mexico, and the United States.
These investigations have been conducted in co-operation with Interpol, through close co-operative ventures such as Franco-American-Canadian meetings on drug enforcement and by sending RCMP investigators to source and transit countries to work on joint international investigations. In addition, the RCMP now has drug investigators stationed in Paris and Hong Kong to assist in international drug information liaison.
I now wish to deal with British Columbia in particular. I am advised that between 60 and 70 per cent of the total illicit drug problem in Canada is centred in British Columbia. Heroin addiction is the major problem, and it is estimated that 10,000 persons are involved in the illicit use of this drug in that province. In the city of Vancouver, a single dose, or capsule of heroin now costs $35. Each person using heroin will purchase an average of two capsules each day. This means that 10,000 heroin users will spend $700,000 each day, or $20 million each month.
During the past two months, 21 Vi pounds of heroin have been seized as a result of drug investigations in British Columbia. The RCMP recently conducted a major undercover operation in the greater Vancouver area during which 25 persons were charged with selling narcotics. Sixteen of those charged were considered to be major international or national drug traffickers. Unfortunately, the magnitude of illicit heroin traffic in British Columbia is such that these recent successful operations have not reduced the current availability of heroin.
There have been new initiatives, however. In British Columbia there are now 107 RCMP federal drug unit positions, of which 69 are assigned to the Vancouver RCMP drug unit. The Vancouver unit is to be increased by 17 positions by April 1, 1975, for a total of 86. The depart-

November 12, 1974
Organized Crime
ment of the attorney general of British Columbia has initiated a new program called CLEU or Co-ordinated Law Enforcement Unit. As part of this program, members of the RCMP and the Vancouver city police work together on major criminal problems. A recent successful drug investigation was concluded by a combined group of 16 RCMP members and nine Vancouver city police members.
Mr. Speaker, I should now like to explain to the House the assistance given by the federal government to the provinces in the form of Royal Canadian Mounted Police, national police, services. The government provides and bears the total cost of a national police service to all Canadian law enforcement agencies as one way of helping to combat crime in Canada. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police is the major and central criminal intelligence body in Canada and must be in a position to provide full and comprehensive facilities for the exchange of criminal intelligence with other police forces. These national police services include: (a) an identification branch and central fingerprint bureau; (b) six crime detection laboratories, located in New Brunswick, Ontario, Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia and Manitoba; (c) the Canadian Police Information Centre; (d) the Criminal Intelligence Service Canada; (e) Interpol; and (f) the Canadian Police College.
Of most direct significance to this debate, particularly as it concerns crime rings and criminal conspiracies, is the Criminal Intelligence Service Canada which I should like to describe in some detail. In 1962, it was decided to create a Canada-wide network of criminal intelligence units to combat the growing problem of organized crime in a coordinated and efficient manner. In 1970, Criminal Intelligence Service Canada was founded and it presently consists of 23 national criminal intelligence sections, six airport special squads, three special surveillance sections and 46 intelligence sections from other police departments and enforcement agencies. Two types of intelligence are handled-strategic intelligence and tactical intelligence. Strategic intelligence confirms the existence of organized crime elements and identifies the members of the group, their criminal activities, internal administration, movements, sources of income and vulnerability. Tactical intelligence is the gaining of information for prosecution and is subject to the rules of evidence.
The Criminal Intelligence Service, because it promotes a close working relationship between police forces, has made possible a number of successful joint force operations. During the past three years, joint force operations have resulted in excess of 250 criminal charges being laid, they have prevented at least two murders and located one of Canada's ten most wanted criminals. In addition, many notable criminals have been identified and a secret organization along the lines of the old mafia code was found to exist in Canada. During the past year, many of the efforts of the Criminal Intelligence Service have been directed toward the high priority areas of drug enforcement and commercial fraud. Hon. members may wish to note that in 1969-70 the national crime intelligence sections numbered 65 men in total. This year, 1974-75, the strength of these sections has been more than doubled to 146 members.
I turn now, Mr. Speaker, to the specific problem of loan sharking, that is, the loaning of money at exorbitant rates

of interest. This is a matter of great concern to the government. I am advised by the RCMP that this is one of the most lucrative practices used by criminals. Loan sharking is difficult to detect, and under current legislation, chiefly involving the Small Loans Act, prosecution is not effective. For this reason my colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), is preparing legislation for revision of the Interest Act. One feature of the proposed new legislation will be the licensing of all persons engaged in the business of lending money.
I am advised that loan sharking is in operation in many of our major cities. There appears to be no set interest rate on such loans; the majority run from 10 per cent to 35 per cent per week on the full amount borrowed. On occasion, criminals involved will borrow money at normal rates of interest and loan it out at exorbitant rates to establish themselves. Loan sharking also breeds other forms of crime, both directly and indirectly. On occasion, loans are made to finance illegal activities such as drug trafficking, gambling and robberies. Indirectly, other crimes are committed by victims as the only means to repay loans. This repayment could take the form of supplying the loan shark with information that can be used to assist in other criminal offences such as robberies. Because of lack of complaints from victims, it is almost impossible for the police authorities to accurately assess the seriousness of loan sharking operations throughout the country. We know a serious problem exists, however, and we propose to concentrate on work in this area.
Before I comment specifically on the matters raised by hon. members opposite, I should like to point out that the Department of the Solicitor General has, itself, as a principal objective, the prevention of crime and the protection of the public. I must remind the House that jurisdiction for the enforcement of the criminal law in Canada is broadly divided between the provincial governments and the federal government. The federal government legislates in the area of criminal law and for the most part the provinces enforce this legislation. The Criminal Code is enforced by provincial attorneys general-

speechtext: Except in the Territories.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE GOVERNMENT ACTION TO COMBAT ORGANIZED CRIME
speechtext:
Except in the Territories; the hon. member is correct. Other criminal law statutes, such as the Narcotics Control Act, are enforced by the federal government. With respect to the courts, judges are appointed by the federal government, and in many of the courts administration is conducted by the provinces. Probation comes under provincial jurisdiction; parole under federal jurisdiction. Jail sentences of less than two years are under provincial jurisdiction; longer sentences are within federal jurisdiction.
So we have a very mixed jurisdiction in the area of criminal law. It is an area where it is extremely important that there be close co-operation not only between the federal and provincial governments but also between the federal, provincial and municipal governments. That having been said, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the federal government should take a leadership role in the criminal justice system. As a result, last year I called the first
November 12, 1974

federal-provincial conference in 14 years dealing with this matter.
The ministry of the Solicitor General, as I have said, is a focal point, or should become more and more the focal point, for the co-ordination and support of the fight against crime. It will support and assist the Commissioner of the RCMP in his efforts to improve co-operation between police forces. It will encourage and attempt to improve federal-provincial co-operation within the criminal justice system, and it will encourage better consultation within the national police community. In addition, it will work toward a common high standard of police training and police technology on a national basis. I should like to point out that one of the major projects of the secretariat of the Solicitor General's ministry is the conference that we are now planning, with the provinces, on the native offender. This conference will be taking place in Alberta some time in the month of February.
I should now like to comment briefly on some of the points made by hon. members opposite. I must congratulate them on the good speeches they have made. I think the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) very well described the problem of organized crime in Canada and its serious consequences. I also appreciated his comment that we must not only look to the symptoms of crime but to the causes of crime; that if we are to be successful in the long run, we must do much more in the area of the causes of crime. I should like to point out to the House that in recent years, through the ministry of the Solicitor General, we have been trying to do just that. We have had interdepartmental committees on crime and housing, dealing with the whole problem of urban renewal, slums and crime. We have had an interdepartmental committee with respect to Indian affairs and the native offender. We have had interdepartmental committees on the drug problem.
The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe recommended a royal commission into the causes of organized crime, and I will take that suggestion under consideration. I can only say that the advice I have from police forces is that a royal commission would not be that useful. They feel that for the most part a probe of this kind is usually overtaken by time and events, and that generally the work of a royal commission is not that useful in assisting the police. On the other hand, I would be willing to consider, and I am considering now, the possibility of a federal-provincial conference on crime and policing. As I pointed out earlier in my remarks, this is an area which concerns the provinces. The hon. member himself said that anything that is done should be done in equal co-operation with the provinces and, as I say, I am considering a federal-provincial conferecne on this particular matter.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) suggested that we should take action, either immediately or as soon as possible, on the recommendations made in the Le Dain report. As hon. members know, the principal responsibility for implementing the recommendations of the Le Dain report comes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). However, we do have an interdepartmental committee working on this particular report. My ministry is involved, other ministries are involved and we will soon have an announcement to make in this respect.
Organized Crime
The hon. member also said that the methods presently used by the RCMP are out of date. He said they were time-worn methods, and he made reference to Japan, Great Britain and other jurisdictions with regard to things we should be doing. As I mentioned earlier in my remarks, we are presently doing some of the things the hon. member suggested, such as international policing, stationing men in other countries and following up on drug trafficking in other countries. In particular, we are participating with the provinces, especially with the province of British Columbia, in regard to CLEU. The hon. member might say that we should do more, and I agree we should and we will try to do more.
The hon. member strongly suggested that we should try to do more in the area of diversion, especially with young offenders. Again, this is a matter we are examining. We are presently working to frame and to put to the House very shortly a new young offenders act to replace the Juvenile Deliquents Act. We are working very closely with the provinces to bring about a system whereby we will be able to provide, in co-operation with the provinces, services and facilities for young offenders.
The hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) concentrated to a great extent on drug traffickers, and I agree with many of the things he said. He said that there was too much tendency nowadays to be sorry for criminals, that too much emphasis was placed on helping criminals. In response, I can only say that we are introducing new programs in the area of rehabilitation-these are sometimes interpreted as being sorry for criminals-because we are hoping we will get to the causes of crime, a matter mentioned by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe. These programs are designed to rehabilitate criminals. We believe that if we are to be serious about protecting the public we must do everything possible to help inmates so that they do not return to crime. I know that very often these programs are considered as being soft on crime, but they are really designed to protect the public.

speechtext: Would the minister permit a question at this point?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE GOVERNMENT ACTION TO COMBAT ORGANIZED CRIME
speechtext: Yes, I would.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE GOVERNMENT ACTION TO COMBAT ORGANIZED CRIME
speechtext: The minister ran through the functions of the various agencies in his department, but he made one glaring omission and that was the police security and planning analysis group, or whatever name the agency is now known by. The name seems to change as rapidly as do some of the faces around here. Would the minister bring us up to date on what part that group is playing in combating organized crime in Canada?

I do not think it was ever known as that. I should like to say a few words about the RCMP and its support of provincial initiatives. The role of the RCMP as the federal law enforcement agency is, in part, to prevent and detect offences against federal statutes and to conduct investigations as required. Enforcement of the Criminal Code is considered for the most part to be within the provincial governments' responsibility for the administration of justice. In saying this, however, I want to point out that in eight of our ten provinces the RCMP act as the provincial police force and in this role is responsible to the respective attorneys general or solicitors general. In the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, in which the RCMP is not the provincial police force, and in the eight contract provinces, I may say that co-operation between the RCMP and provincial authorities is excellent.
I might illustrate this by pointing out that through the national Criminal Intelligence Service, and in other ways, the RCMP have responded to recent provincial initiatives, such as the Quebec commission of inquiry into organized crime, the Ontario inquiry into organized crime and the building trades, and the recent work of the British Columbia co-ordinated law enforcement unit.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE GOVERNMENT ACTION TO COMBAT ORGANIZED CRIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the mover, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner), first of all for bringing this resolution before the House today. I can say with all modesty that I had nothing to do with its formulation or the very stable, very restrained and very philosophical approach the hon. member took in his speech in which he outlined in a very sympathetic way the causes of crime in the country. It was a speech well worth making, and I quite frankly say to him, through you, Mr. Speaker, that I envy his oratorical powers and the way in which he made his speech. It was a speech well worth making. It is about time somebody said what the hon. member said today about crime, and I most heartily agree with him.
Let me say again, attempting to use the most restrained language possible, that I found the minister's reply today very disappointing. Now that we have had the philosophical approach from the hon. member, indicating the causes of organized crime in this country, I would suggest that my role now is to indicate in some small way the inroads organized crime has already made in this country.
I think the attitude displayed by the minister here today was good, as far as he went, but as is usual with most things we hear from across the floor of this chamber, I must say in all sincerity that his statement today was extremely disappointing and lacking in real depth as to just what has happened in this country in the last decade. I suggest that is indicated, as well, by the attendance here today. We have the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who was here for the question period but who quickly left, and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) who I suggest should be playing a supervisory role in this whole matter but who has not even put in an attendance today. I would indicate to the minister, as well, that I am disappointed that he has to leave in approximately five minutes as he indicated earlier.
Traditionally, in fighting crime in this country the provincial and local presence has been paramount. In the last decade especially, sophisticated uses of communications and transportation techniques by warped but intelligent men have of necessity left provincial, municipal and local law enforcement agencies far behind and virtually helpless in combating internationally-directed and syndicated organized crime. This is true, not because of lack of intent, and in many cases not because of lack of training, but simply because of their limited, restricted jurisdiction. The minister may point with pride to the divided jurisdiction in combating crime in this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE GOVERNMENT ACTION TO COMBAT ORGANIZED CRIME
speechtext: Not with pride. That is our system.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE GOVERNMENT ACTION TO COMBAT ORGANIZED CRIME
speechtext:
The minister may point to the system in an attempt to defend it, but I find it almost indefensible. I think we are wavering, in this country, under an extremely archaic system, one that has certainly not kept up with the times. I think the place from which initiative and leadership should come is here in Ottawa. Initiative and leadership should come from the federal government toward changing the system, because the system is clearly wrong. I think the federal government and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police should have become far more paramount and should be the priority law enforcement agency. This government should be the government con-
November 12, 1974

cerned with combating organized crime in this country. It should be far more innovative and far more supervisory in leading the fight against organized crime, in a way that so far simply has not surfaced.

When I have finished I will be glad to entertain questions. At a time when crime statistics in this country are far more than merely alarming, and at a time when obviously there is international control and foreign direction to what is going on in this country in respect of crime, the reverse is true of this government. Initiative and leadership on the part of this government is absolutely nil, and this has been demonstrated time and time again.
Over the last decade the morale in the RCMP has deteriorated to the point now that the RCMP is no longer the proud and effective force it once was. The leadership which emanates from this government has sadly deteriorated. We need more political direction. The law enforcement agencies need more money, more help, more facilities, experts and professional people. They are simply not getting that type of leadership, they are not getting that type of financial help and they are not getting the direction they need. I suggest this is not only true of the RCMP. Our Customs and Excise Branch has simply stood still for the last 50 years. Generally speaking, the Department of Revenue investigators are simply incompetent, due to their lack of training and lack of knowledge of what has been going on in the past. I think they sincerely and genuinely need far more facilities, better training and better pay. I think, as well, they need university and research assistance in ways they are not getting it at the moment.
I think this is the reason for the debate today. This is an honest attempt by the opposition, using the only means available to it at the moment, to wake a sleepy, lethargic government out of its apathy. Today we are seeing the effects of that apathy. At the moment we have, at the most, 20 government members in the House. I suggest that we have had a very lethargic and sleepy reply from a mediocre minister. For instance, why did he not deal with the involvement of organized crime in the construction industry labour unions and in other industries which has become apparent in the last 18 months in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario? It is nonsense on the part of the minister or anyone else to suggest that this whole matter is subject only to provincial jurisdiction. We have had royal commissions in both provinces-one is still continuing-which indicate in no uncertain terms that organized crime is now linked with the construction industry in both Ontario and Quebec.
Royal Canadian Mounted Police investigations alone have linked certain underworld figures with the violence which plagued the industry two years ago, and last year in James Bay approximately $8,000 of syndicate money supported local 791 in its strike at an estimated cost of over $1 million in the $26 million road construction project. Known, internationally-syndicated "soldiers" were also

employed on this side at the time. But today we have no comment, no information, no suggestion whatsoever from the minister. Why did he not deal today with the white-collar crime which is rampant?

We are not dealing with peanuts; we are dealing with an industry which in Ontario alone deals in hundreds of millions of dollars annually.' speechtext:
As I said, Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the courtesy of the House and I hope I shall not trespass unduly. There are a number of subjects that one would want to get into in a wide-ranging debate such as this, but I want to deal with two, if I may. One is the question of whether organized crime has infiltrated the very ranks of government itself. I should like to bring to the attention of the House the case of Mr. Charles Spatero who at one time was from Buffalo, New York. Dilly, as he is known to his friends, is what is known in the trade as a "torch". A torch is a gentleman who specializes in incendiary and arson work in Toronto, Montreal and some of our larger areas.
For the last little while there has been an alarming outbreak of arson. It is connected, obviously, with loan sharking, obviously with protection rackets and obviously with the enforcement of underworld regulations and judgments. They do exist, Mr. Speaker. I should like to suggest to you that so far in this session, in any event, I have heard no explanation whatsoever from the government or the minister as to the rather novel and alarming series of events that have overtaken Mr. Charles Angelo Spatero. He was sentenced in 1970 to the maximum sentence for arson in this country, 14 years, by Judge Martin in Toronto. On June 15, while incarcerated in Warkworth prison-which is just outside the boundaries of my riding-Mr. Spatero managed to obtain a three-day pass in order to see his wife who was supposed to be in a motel nearby.
Here is a man who received the maximum sentence on a charge of arson, Mr. Speaker. The evidence at the trial clearly indicated that he was not just on trial for one charge, but in actual fact there were five different related charges of arson. The one they got Dilly on was for pouring alcohol and gasoline all through a crowded tavern in downtown Toronto. In any event, he got 14 years. Somehow, somewhere, a man with that record got a three-day weekend pass on June 15. I do not find that remarkable because there are many other instances of people such as that getting weekend passes today. This is a novel technique that was brought about by the Trudeau government in this country. I am not so sure it has been a success, but that is not the point I am worried about today.
On June 15, on that weekend pass, of course, Dilly Spatero never returned to the Warkworth prison. Before long it was obvious that he had got into a green Cadillac- registered to a known underworld figure in New York state-in Campbellford which is just a few miles away from the prison, and obviously he was across the border in a matter of hours. That was known to law enforcement agencies in New York state, to law enforcement agencies in Canada; and it was known, as well, by the newspapers. Actually, on October 23 the reporters of two Toronto newspapers interviewed Mr. Spatero in Buffalo, New York. The point is that he was an escaped arsonist, a dangerous man. That was even the opinion of the late Mr. Maggadino, the crime boss in Buffalo who controlled certain kinds of crime in Hamilton and Toronto. Mr. Maggadino is no longer alive, but his organization is still alive. This man, Spatero, is a recognized torch. He should not have been out on weekend leave. He was out, and he got away. There has been an unaccountable delay in serving extradition papers in respect of Mr. Spatero.

November 12, 1974
Organized Crime
Let me go over the facts again. In 1970 he was convicted and sent up for 14 years. On June 15 he escaped. Not until July were extradition papers finally signed by the Department of Justice in Ottawa. But absolutely nothing was done with those papers. Mr. Spatero was in Buffalo and everyone knew he was in Buffalo. The New York state people were doing their utmost to pin something on him so that he could be put away, because he is a recognized, dangerous figure. Reporters from the Toronto Star and the Toronto Sun interviewed him on October 25. At the same time, sir, the district attorney in Buffalo publicly indicated his displeasure because the authorities could not nail him for anything. The papers from Ottawa simply had never reached Washington. Hence, they had never gone from Washington to Buffalo because they were not in the United States.
It looks to me as if this case goes far beyond mere bureaucratic bungling in Ottawa. What happened goes beyond coincidence. I could give more examples like this, but will not bore the House with them. Events like this, linked with some of the difficulties encountered by the RCMP in Quebec, lead one to the inescapable conclusion that organized crime has put great pressure even on governments, even on our law enforcement agencies. Have we heard any worth-while explanation from the minister regarding the activities of Mr. Samson, the RCMP officer in Montreal who was involved in the July 26 bombing of one of the directors of Steinberg's?

Injured in the attempt, he is reputed to have been in contact both with Camille Gervais and William Obrunt. Gervais is awaiting sentence for conspiracy, while Obrunt has been designated by police as an underworld banker. Obrunt has been missing at least since October 16, 1974, and still does not seem to have been located. This leaves us with two questions: where is Obrunt now, and what does the government intend to do to find him and to prosecute him? I say that the Samson affair ties in with another alleged link to organized crime. RCMP officers McLery and Brunet were fired from the force in December, 1973, apparently due to their association-with whom? With Mr. Obrunt. They attempted to have their case reviewed but ran into difficulty when told that all relevant facts would be made public. They then decided not to have their case reviewed. I do not know where the pressure for that came from, whether it came from the underworld or from the RCMP; but no matter where the pressure came from, the circumstances look suspicious and the government owes us an explanation. All three of these men were involved with intelligence and with security.
On October 24, only eight days after they gave evidence that Samson was somehow connected with the underworld, it was announced that the FBI and the CIA had been asked to aid with security for the Olympic Games. The timing is too obvious to be ignored. The hypothesis is that by infiltrating the RCMP, organized crime was able to get hold of the security plans for the Olympics. Obvi-

ously, these plans would be sold to the highest terrorist bidders in the world.
I will not deal with the computation of crimes: we can deal with that another day. Let me say that I echo the sentiments which have been expressed in this debate. Our aim in this country should be to increase the deterrent to crime by increasing the chance of detection. We do not necessarily need to increase the length of jail terms or their severity. I completely agree with the thrust of the speech made by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe. We need more work, more leadership, more initiative to be shown by the government in combating crime and its causes. If we can do that best by establishing a royal commission, we should establish that royal commission. The minister suggested that royal commissions, according to police experts, are not the best way of assisting the police. A royal commission might not assist the police, but it would wake up a lethargic and apathetic government and demonstrate the existence of difficulties in this area.
I suggest that we need more co-operation and communication among federal, provincial and local police forces; that we need improved co-operation and communication among federal and provincial departments of justice, prosecutors and officials. For heaven's sake, the provincial Crown Attorney system is there; why duplicate it at the federal level by establishing a new list of federal Crown Attorneys? The police need to concentrate on serious crimes involving victims, and we must investigate the feasibility of removing from the Criminal Code crimes which do not involve victims; crimes such as gambling, prostitution, liquor offences, and so on. Further, RCMP law enforcement officers are too important to be wasted. They should be given better training, and their time should not be wasted in patrolling Ottawa's NCC roads and handing out tickets for driving offences. They should be the experts trained to combat crime. Today, that is simply not the case.
One could make many suggestions. Most of all, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice, and the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) must be aware of what is going on today. They must demonstrate their inherent desire to come to grips with the problem. That, sir, we have not seen.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) for bringing before us a matter which all of us, including the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), consider to be of urgent concern.
None of us like the thought of invasion of our privacy and the taking over of our daily lives by crime syndicates, or habits promoted by them. By the same token I believe there are different ways to tackle this problem.
Many members have concentrated on police work or our laws. I tend to believe we are being a little more than unfair if we are continually to make references to those who have served us, and attempted to serve us well, by saying they are not serving us. Many of our policemen and police forces are doing a great service for us. This is recognized in each community. Indeed, many of our laws are framed in a way which were intended to help.
Unfortunately, this is somewhat of a two-edged sword. Sometimes in the framing of a law, someone uses life like a rock, and the law as a chisel, and tries to carve it in their own likeness. Then they try to impose on others their thoughts as to how life should be.
Some of us look on life as an ocean, and on the laws as sandcastles which crumble as the ocean moves. We hope there will be some around us and among those who make our laws and enforce them, who have this kind of under-

standing. I reject the idea that discipline will get us respect. I believe discipline is the result of respect. Therefore I believe the discipline demanded by society must to a great extent be achieved by itself.
Far too little has been said about the young in this discussion. Who are all these people who sell these drugs? Who are all these people in Vancouver? Who are all these people in the Atlantic provinces? Who are all these people in Montreal?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE GOVERNMENT ACTION TO COMBAT ORGANIZED CRIME
speechtext: Ask the minister. He should know.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE GOVERNMENT ACTION TO COMBAT ORGANIZED CRIME
speechtext:
Are they people none of us will ever know? Are they people that only the minister or a police officer or a judge will know? Are we not the ones who must take the responsibility, rather than placing it on the shoulders of someone else? At what point do we accept this responsibility? At what point do we ask ourselves whether they are juvenile delinquents or whether they are the result of delinquent adults?
The hon. member for Sainte-Hyacinthe comes from an area I knew very well, which I was familiar with, Verdun, Quebec. I remember that we organized a series of open-air dances in co-operation with the police, though after a good deal of opposition from other quarters. We noticed that the incidence of delinquency dropped on those evenings. The police stopped the traffic for the young people; they became friends of the young people, servants of the young people, and servants of the community. As a result the young people respected them. Basically, a healthy respect existed in that community between the young people and the police force.
The Le Dain Commission Report was not the be all and end all as far as drugs are concerned. Many things have changed since that report was issued. It is about time many of us, including policemen and citizens generally, read more about drugs and discovered that this is only a passing history.
I do recall one passage in the report-it did not appear to receive wide publicity at the time-about the situation in one of the maritime provinces. It appears that the citizens did not know what was going on, and even the mayor of Moncton did not know what was going on, but when a questionnaire was sent to one of the schools they discovered that 60 per cent of the young people had experienced soft drugs, acid, or hard drugs. No one mentioned that 85 per cent of the teachers were involved. This was in a small community. I wonder what might be happening in a large community such as the one I come from, Mr. Speaker.
I am not afraid to say for the record that the people of Hamilton Mountain are concerned. They are so concerned that they have started a full-scale drug education program. They have set up a community centre with special courses for nurses, doctors and social workers who attend. They believe they should be dealing with the situation from a knowledge of drugs and the circumstances in which they are taken. Too often I hear it said that the law should take care of these offenders.
I have nothing to say against lawyers, but I must face the fact that when standing before the court each one of them can only see how correct he is-not one is called upon to question his personal position when defending a
November 12, 1974

drug trafficker. The time is coming when we shall be obliged to make a decision, not as legislators, or policemen, or lawyers, but as people who should count ourselves as part of the authority, or force, which serves all of us.
The excellent recommendations which come from the universities from time to time should be adopted, along with other worthwhile suggestions from members of police forces and interested citizens. Members of the community generally should talk about these things and make their contributions toward the decision process.
I respect the views which have been put forward during this debate. Regardless .of our feelings when we oppose each other for policital reasons, I believe that from time to time something will come before this House with which we can all be concerned. I am sure that those who follow me in this debate will have many more informed and intelligent things to say about the subject than I have, and I shall listen attentively.
The time has come to recognize that the way to law and order, the way to deal with the Godfather image, is through education. I believe that basically young people have a liking for and a respect for policemen. Many times that respect is taken from them by the courts, or by those in authority, or by people who seek for their own purposes to make the law or the police force look incorrect, regardless of the effect on the young.
I found that basically there was a kindred feeling between young people and policemen. Basically, you played ball in the streets, when you were too poor to have a dime, and you used the centre sewer as home plate and the two side sewers as third and first base. When a policeman came to move you he moved you as few times as he could, provided it didn't endanger your life. He didn't come driving down the street with a siren to arrest you. So many times in the past policemen have done this, and they are still doing it.
We should look to the policemen, Mr. Speaker. They must be involved in this education process. We should hear what they have to say about some of the measures we have passed as legislators. We should hear why they believe some of those measures do not help them in their tasks. We must seek ways of bringing together all the people who are most deeply involved. We should look upon policemen as those who serve us, respect them for what they do, and give them the opportunity to voice their opinion. I think many young people want this.
If I might just close with one thought in connection with any revision of our law which may take place, I would say this: there is a man by the name of George Raymond, the author and owner of the television show, "This is the Law". In September 1974, while researching material for a film concerning the Canadian children of alcoholic parents, Mr. Raymond was awakened to the depressing dilemma of hundreds of thousands of children in this country who are mentally and physically abused by an alcoholic parent, every day of their young lives.
Overwhelmed by the enormity of this single area of child neglect, and having in mind in the very broadest sense the myriad of other problems and decisions a child is compelled to face by himself, alone, every day, due to parental and public indifference, he was inspired to write

"The Rights of Man." The words are by George Raymond, the music by Tommy Ambrose.
So much has been said 'bout the Rights of Man Since the time when that man could first write,
Since he moved from his cave to the light of the day And he yearned for the land which was so far far away Since he learned how to work-how to love-how to play.
He's been worried 'bout his personal rights.
So much has been said 'bout the Rights of Man Since he first came aware of his might,
Look at all that Man's done since he climbed from his tree How he's learned how to walk-how to sail on the sea How he's jumped on the moon with such obvious glee,
Always worried 'bout his personal rights.
So much has been said 'bout the Rights of Man Since priorities gave him a fright,
Since man learned how to add and subtract and divide His material wealth-which he often would hide While he figured the wealth of the opposite side,
He's been worried 'bout his personal rights.
So much has been said 'bout the Rights of Man Since he first felt his halo grow tight,
How man said "If it's there-then it's good for us all"
So he worked and invented and prospered-grew tall Or drew strength from some bottle to soften his fall,
Always worried 'bout his personal rights.
So much has been said 'bout the Rights of Man Since the time when man first said "I'm right",
'bout the wonderful things man has said and then done Since he first grew his food-since he harnessed the sun How he's spread the good word since inventing the gun,
Always worried 'bout his personal rights.
So much has been said 'bout the Rights of Man Since his genius first helped win his fights,
Look at all that he's done since he first turned the sod How he's crippled and killed for some great nameless god How he despoils his children while using the rod.
Always worried 'bout his personal rights.
But what of the rights of The Child of Man As man dreams of his personal wealth?
The young child who's ignored both in body and mind Who is lonely and hungry and cold and can't find Any shelter or love in a world where he's tossed,
To be shot-to be burned-to be bombed-to be lost.
Yes, what of the rights of The Child of Man As man hurried through life to his fate?
While preoccupied man carries on with neglect Of his children-while showing the highest respect For the power and might of the sword and the gun,
And the pitiful acre dead bodies just won.
So what of the rights of The Child of Man As man scratches along to his goals?
Where consumption of his all consuming desire Where the dollar and status will kindle his fire To be first-to be fastest and biggest-why not?
Who has time for the plight of some faceless young tot?

I think we have to look to those who make money out of drugs. We have to look to those who have the power to direct others. But I do say that each and every one of us has the responsibility to think of the rights of children at this time. If our laws could in some way be expressed, they would be expressed by what most of us when we were young saw, and what most of us see now-a policeman holding the hand of a small child.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE GOVERNMENT ACTION TO COMBAT ORGANIZED CRIME
speechtext:
I am grateful that you allowed me to call it six o'clock a minute or two before that hour so that my trend of thought, if that is the expression, would not be interruped.
I think it is useful for this House of Commons to spend a day debating a matter or an issue which is of very great concern to a good number of Canadians. I want to congratulate my colleague, the hon. member for Saint-Hya-cinthe (Mr. Wagner), for a very constructively argued contribution to this debate. His argument seemed to me to be progressive and positive.
When we are considering the whole issue of crime, Mr. Speaker, we have to keep slogans to a minimum. Simplistic solutions really do not help us at all. After all, the last person to use law and order as an election gimmick, the last person to use this over-simplified and pejorative phrase, the last campaign which aroused the public into a state of frenzy about law and order was that of Richard Nixon, a Richard Nixon who subverted law while invoking a slogan. We have a very great deal to learn from the very unhappy experience of the United States about what I would call an over-simple view of a terribly complex issue.
There is nothing new, of course, in organized crime, and for the purpose of this debate I think of organized crime as crime organized on a continental or worldwide basis. However, what is new, it seems to me, is the amount of technological sophistication which those engaged in organized crime are able to use for their nefarious purposes.
We have heard from our colleague, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt), and we have also read the statistics about the very grave phenomena of the drug problem of British Columbia. We have learned with horror the fact that drug addiction has increased by something like 455 per cent in the last five years in the province of British Columbia. In other words, the total there is approximately two-thirds of the national total in hard drug terms. The drug trade there has mushroomed into a

half billion dollar business, and some eight syndicates in the lower mainland have used the proceeds of the drug trade to have money laundered through legitimate businesses.
Mention has already been made of the Co-ordinated Law Enforcement Unit, an enterprise, as I understand it, of the Attorney General of British Columbia. It is a cooperative effort by metropolitan Vancouver, British Columbia and the RCMP, but the spark came from the Attorney General of British Columbia.
That group found that "gang money", as they call it, is being "laundered" through legitimate business enterprises throughout the province. Law enforcement agencies estimate that up to 30 per cent of the mining and local junior industrial companies on the Vancouver stock exchange are in danger of being manipulated by criminally oriented promoters who are getting away virtually scotfree. The report also cites the securities industry, the second mortgage field and nightclubs as the three other areas that might be called legitimate businesses in their organization and concept, yet have been infiltrated by what might be termed "dirty" money.
Statistics Canada figures, from law enforcement, judicial and correctional statistics, support the agonizing situation, if I can use that adjective, in British Columbia. Statistics Canada goes on to describe the totals for Canada. It states:
Each of the four drug classifications continue to show an increase nationally from a low of 17.2 per cent for addicting opiate like drugs to a high of 106.8 per cent (101.0 per cent in the first half of 1973) for Cannabis (Marijuana) related offences.
While the percentage change for three of the four drug offences varied substantially from large increases to significant decreases in the provinces, all provinces showed an increase in the Cannabis classification from a low of 27.4 per cent in Prince Edward Island, to a high of 127.3 per cent in Ontario.
Some hon. members have made the suggestion that for drug trafficking we should return to capital punishment. I have taken part in two capital punishment debates in this parliament, and I have no doubt at all that capital punishment is not a deterrent to drug trafficking or anything else. As the hon. member for New Westminster reminded us, there are now very severe penalties, such as life imprisonment, for drug trafficking.
There is just one other statistic that I would like to share. There is one element of the crime picture in Canada that has taken a somewhat positive turn, and that is that the murder rate in this country in 1974 is substantially less than in 1973 by some 15 per cent. In 1973, the rate was lower than in 1972. I just put these statistics on the record as a footnote to remind some hon. members that, whether or not capital punishment is abolished, the violent crime of murder is on the decrease in Canada. I am sorry to say, and hon. members probably know this, that other forms of violent crime have in fact increased over the last few years.
What should be done about organized crime? I believe, as do several hon. members who have spoken, that our aim should be to increase the deterrent by increasing the chances of detection. I think that this is the key, and several hon. members have made this point. There is really
November 12, 1974

not much point in increasing the length of jail terms or their severity-they are already very severe. I think we need several things and I should like to share my thoughts with hon. members.
First, we need improved co-operation and communication between federal, provincial and local police forces, and I think the key example, of which several hon. members have spoken, that operates in British Columbia is a very positive thing.
Second, we need improved co-operation and communication between federal and provincial justice departments, prosecutors and officials. I share the view of the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) that it is too bad that we are into the business of proliferating the office of the Crown Attorney. There are excellent Crown Attorneys working in the provinces. It is a pity that these officials have not had the responsibility of prosecuting narcotics offences and that the patronage system has been operating in this federal field. Many law enforcement people to whom I have spoken have deplored this because they feel that Crown Attorneys build up a body of jurisprudence, a body of expertise, and could well handle this and other federal offences.
Third, we need the concentration by police on serious crimes involving a victim.
Fourth, we need an investigation of the feasibility of the gradual removal of victimless crimes from the statute books, such as gambling, prostitution, liquor offences, and so on. The police are now being used as sort of moral guides, and in many cases the morals which they are trying to enforce have become outdated by changed public attitudes. That does not say that all our attitudes with regard to these things have changed, but it means that in general the police are expected in some cases to be watchdogs over morality rather than involved in the much more serious business of investigating crimes where there is a victim.
Fifth, should my last suggestion be adopted, of course this would free prison space and also free the police.
Sixth, we must free trained policemen from the need to handle minor traffic offences, family quarrels, and so on. The police now are expected to cover the whole gamut of serious and grave crimes from murder to whether someone overstayed their time in a parking spot.
Seventh, I suggest that we need to investigate measures to make criminals pay restitution for their acts to victims, as recommended last week by the Law Reform Commission in a most interesting report. I will come back to that report in a minute. At present the victim is often penalized physically or financially for life, while the criminal is in jail for a short term.
Eighth, only when we are certain that victims are protected should we concern ourselves with what we might call the general welfare of the criminal, although this also must be put in perspective.
Ninth, the best deterrent is not inhumane punishment but the certainty of detection. I do not know whether any hon. members listened last night to a radio program where a person who has just come out after nine years in Dorchester, the maximum security penitentiary, kept repeating that he was not sure about the rehabilitation in Dor-
Organized Crime
Chester but he was very certain that what would prevent him from repeating his crime was the fear of detection. Lastly, I think we should remember that detection rates are very low in this country, that the courts are overcrowded and that punishment is seriously varied depending on where you are located.
I was going to say that punishment is also dependent on whom you know, but I do not think that is the case. I think it is a fact that a variety of people are responsible for punishment. I think that the Department of the Solicitor General is to be commended for the efforts they and the Justice Department have made toward getting supreme court and county judges and magistrates together to discuss the matter of sentencing, because I think that the variety of sentences handed out for similar crimes in this country makes cynics, not only of those caught but of many of us who practice law.
I was interested in the third report of the Law Reform Commission for a couple of reasons. First of all, it is well written. In a very few pages it sets out some recommendations and some conclusions that had been reached by the commission since its second annual report. It is a pleasure to read a document prepared by officials that is written in elegant English, and presumably the same goes for the other official language, French. It happened that the original of this report was written-and I took the trouble to find out-by Professor Patrick Fitzgerald of Carleton University.
A surprising number of people have spoken to me about the elegant or, more than that, the very clear, direct, understandable and pleasant language. I wish everybody in offices in this national capital could read this report. I do think that there are all too few reports produced in government departments that have any lasting quality. Anyway, it is the report of the commission, no matter who wrote it. The commission reminds us:
Reforming laws means more than changing them; it means improving them. The two don't always go together. Cromwell's Parliament once passed an act outlawing Christmas-a change admittedly but was it an improvement? Was the new law a true reflection of the social need?
All I could do here is interpolate that if anybody were to pass a law outlawing Christmas until Christmas, I think it would be an improvement. This is away off the subject and I am ready to be taken to task for it right away, but it did remind me that we seem to start Christmas right after Halloween now.
To get back to the point, Mr. Speaker, the commission goes on to ask how we can ensure that new laws truly reflect the social need?
The report reminds us that in ancient Greece somebody who had a proposal to make for a change in the law was brought forward with a yoke around his neck. He then had to debate the change and if he were successful in persuading the citizens he was freed and, if not, he suffered the consequences. Nobody would propose such a drastic thing in 1974, I hope, but I thought that the commission report gave a rather thoughtful analysis of the difficulty of law reform.

November 12, 1974
Organized Crime
Anybody can propose an amendment to a statute. All that is needed is paste, a pair of scissors and a parliament that is-I will not say lazy because this parliament has not been going long enough for me to make any judgment on that. But it is easy enough to change the criminal law by patchwork. To change the philosophy behind the law without the public understanding and support which are essential, is much more difficult.
I myself happen to have voted for and supported with enthusiasm the change in the provisions for bail. But, Mr. Speaker, we parliamentarians made a very grave mistake about that law because we did not take the trouble and the time to instruct the law enforcement agencies in the use of the changed rule, and did not perform our duty by taking our case-or the government's case since the credit rightfully belongs to the government-for this good reform to the public to get an understanding of it.
The Law Reform Commission discussed a couple of things that we are working on, and I will end on this note as I see Mr. Speaker is getting very nervous. In working papers Nos. 5 and 6 the Law Reform Commission made two very worthwhile recommendations. Working paper No. 5 dealt with restitution and compensation for the victims of crime, and working paper No. 6 dealt with fines rather than incarceration. The commission did a very wise and more than humane thing-I know some people will think I am being sentimental when indeed I am anything but-indeed I think a sentence to jail is often a copout. In many cases it is much easier to go to jail than to pay the restitution or a fine.
I think if the government sees fit to accept these recommendations on restitution, compensation and fines, a lot of the pressures on our penitentiary system could be relieved and the police could get on with their real business, that is, dealing with the grave and serious crimes about which many of my colleagues on both sides of the House have reminded us today.

I am very happy that the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) brought this matter up because it has been of deepest concern to me for many, many years. I have worked on the problem of drugs, on juvenile crime-all crime right through to murder- throughout my entire career of 30 years. I am glad the hon. member brought it up as a non-partisan issue, one that every person in this chamber should be concerned about. Every family in this country, every father and mother- everyone-has been touched by this.
There was a day when I was a rarity because I knew criminals, and I knew them as a white collar worker. Today everybody knows a drug user, either in their own family or in the neighbourhood. It is the great devastation of our time; it can destroy the very fabric of our society if it continues.
I am also very grateful to my compatriot, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt), who recorded most accurately the problem in the west, one that is

now spreading throughout the country. I do not agree with everything he said, but I agree in part.
If oratory could solve the horrendous problem of mass killing by drug dealers, once known as merchants of death, it would have been solved this afternoon in this House of Commons.
I am deeply concerned that some hon. members are so out of touch that they believe the drug scene is the syndrome of the poor. It is not, Mr. Speaker; it is a problem of all classes of society, particularly the middle and upper classes.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE GOVERNMENT ACTION TO COMBAT ORGANIZED CRIME
speechtext: That is why we are dealing with it now.

As a newcomer here I understand now why this disease has been allowed to spread and contaminate the whole country-why children have been affected and disabled by the time they reach their majority. They deteriorated and died on the streets. I watched it, Mr. Speaker. That is why I find this debating and playing games with such a serious problem so absolutely abhorrent.
I was appalled that the hon. member for Northumber-land-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) made this a political debate when he, as Attorney General of the Province of Ontario only a few years ago, could have resolved many of the problems that are now endemic in Canada.

speechtext: Don't get political!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE GOVERNMENT ACTION TO COMBAT ORGANIZED CRIME
speechtext:
As a citizen of this great country I was saddened to think that a problem as serious as this could be treated as a matter of oratory. I hope I am not included in that because there is much I want to tell members from my experience working on the streets of Vancouver, on Mountain Avenue in Montreal, Yorkville in Toronto, Osborne Street in Winnipeg and in Calgary. I worked in Haight-Ashbury; I worked in Aspen, Colorado; and the lower east side of New York to research this problem. I have researched the basic causes of violence. So I come here not for oratory but to tell this House that we have a problem which everyone of us must put our minds to in order to solve it.
I begged for help in 1966, Mr. Speaker. I went across this country as it was exploding, and asked for help. But I was accused of being an alarmist. I tried to explain that when a house is burning and children are inside, we do not stand back and wait.
Nine year olds are now mainlining drugs and heroin. In British Columbia, 65 per cent of addicts are under 18 years of age. We are talking of children, Mr. Speaker. I can remember when I wrote a news story about a 17-year old girl using heroin and it ran on page one. That was only ten years ago, Mr. Speaker.
I can remember in the drug wars of 1955-56. When I worked behind the scenes with users, pushers and police, they only used bombs because there were just two syndicates. Now there are probably seven or eight, because the market is big enough to support them all.
November 12, 1974

We should be fortunate in Canada if there were only
15,000	addicts in this country. Statistics compiled by the new Co-ordinating Law Enforcement Unit, called CLEU in British Columbia, show that the average drug user uses an average of two caps a day, and that heroin addiction progresses and gets worse. In the old days you heard people talk of going "cold turkey", which was a painful experience. It simply meant that a user was trying to cut back to, say, one cap a day. In those days he paid $5 for a cap; today's price is between $35 and $40. If the user could stay on two caps a day, he thought it a miracle.
In almost every neighbourhood of Vancouver, Victoria, Nanaimo or Prince Rupert, actually in practically every village and town of British Columbia, you will find addicts. There is a well known corner in Vancouver where many known addicts used to congregate. The addict population remained stable for 10 or 12 years. Of the 3,300 known addicts in Canada, two thirds could be found in that neighbourhood of Vancouver. Today the addict population is much larger and the problem is much more serious. Young addicts are using between 15 and 20 caps a day, some as many as 35 caps. You can work out the arithmetic of the massive use and see how much crime results from a habit this big.
There has been so much oratory in this chamber today that perhaps it is time to put before hon. members some basic facts about the drug situation. I am aware of various facets of the law. I am not a lawyer but have worked in the streets and have been involved in observing nearly every facet of crime. I have worked in the courts, in the prisons, on parole cases, in the streets with addicts, and with hippies. They have even crashed my living room. I talked freely to them and learned from them. I have been close to the judiciary, to the legal profession and to the police doing law enforcement. I plan to go back to the streets again soon to bring my knowledge up to date. I spent half a day in Vancouver two weeks ago to obtain up-to-date information. I used to go out regularly, once a month, to find out what had happened since the drug scene exploded in 1966.
Today, following the drug user explosion which took place in Vancouver in 1966 and, to a lesser degree, in Toronto and Montreal, there is hardly a street in British Columbia on which you will not find drugs. Originally, of course, drugs simply meant heroin. There was little marijuana or cannabis about. Now you will find MDA, a high powered acid, amphetamines, particularly one called speed which kills-as they know in Toronto-cocaine, which we have not seen in British Columbia for 40 years, opium, the old time drug and elephant weed or Thai stick. How many of you have heard of that powerful form of cannabis?
In addition you will find cannabis in various forms. People say the drug is harmless, less dangerous than alcohol. Let me say here and now that alcohol is indeed the most dangerous drug. Who can say that if cannabis were to be freely available in society in the same manner as alcohol is freely available we will not see 750,000 cannabis addicts? If I had time I would tell you the damage cannabis does.
Organized Crime
Much research has been done into cannabis for the past 30 years. The term cannabis may cover various forms of the drug. For instance, there is marijuana, which varies in strength and degree of effectiveness. I am putting this simply because some members may not be aware of what is happening. Some having started need more and stronger cannabis. Others say, "If you have not tried it, don't knock it." I have not tried it. It is against the law, and it should stay that way.

It varies in strength, depending on where it was grown, under what temperature conditions and so on. Hashish has long been known as the assassin's drug. It is 10 times as strong as ordinary marijuana. Liquid hashish is 10 times as strong as plain hashish, or 100 times stronger than marijuana.
What has happened? Despite the protestations of swingers in our society who want to be "with it", who said that cannabis is not dangerous, the number of addicts has increased from 3,300, of whom 2,200 were in that notorious area of Vancouver, to God knows what number nowadays. You will find their numbers increased dramatically in the two major cities of eastern Canada, and now, as I say, there are God knows how many addicts. You cannot walk on any street in downtown Vancouver in B.C. without seeing them.
There is a difference between the heroin addict of the old days and the modern addict. The old addict was euphoric, without the courage to engage in violence. To obtain drugs the old addict went into prostitution, shoplifting or burglary. At that time a cap cost only $5. Today the western addict is the way the New York addict has been for many years, a violent, dangerous killer. Studies show that the New York addict progressed, in the main, from cannabis to heroin. At least 70 per cent have followed that path. I am certain that the use of a combination of drugs is responsible for the emergence of violence in Vancouver.
Many professionals-doctors, lawyers, social workers, academics and other "with it" people-tried to ingratiate themselves with the young by "doing their thing". Unfortunately, the problem grew too big for the police to handle. Young people started to call the police pigs and, as you will recall, the police countered by saying, "If you are in trouble call a hippy." The police of Vancouver have done a good job, and they could do much better if their efforts were not nullified by the courts. They want people to help them. No doubt we need a larger force to cope with the problem. Often they need to do one job three times, largely because of the work of judges and lawyers.
The courts are not working to resolve the problem. Their actions are aggravating it. The police will work as much as five years gathering evidence through intensive surveillance for a charge or series of charges. The arrest is made and, within a few hours, bail is set and the accused is out on the street. These people have to intensify their drug pushing. They have to raise more money to pay their lawyer or, if there is a possibility of incarceration, to take off to somewhere else. Judges have handed down almost minimal sentences. The court of appeal recently reversed a sentence handed down by a provincial judge who had

sentenced a major pusher to a fine of $15,000 with three years to pay or five months in jail. A major drug pusher can raise $15,000 within a month.
Let me tell you how quickly drug pushers can grow rich. Several years ago I was involved with a motorcycle gang.

I will show you how to use a chain some day, if I really get rough. This young punk I am thinking of could not even afford his 50 cent initiation fee into a motorcycle gang- that's how poor he was. He could not afford to pay his dues at one time. Today, as a non-user pusher, he has at least five pieces of real estate in Vancouver and drives the latest model Mercedes-Benz.
In the spring of 1966 I began a book on teenagers. I discussed the changing morality of the young. I had two paragraphs dealing with LSD and marijuana. Then came Dr. Timothy Leary of Harvard, the great guru of the psychedelic cult, and all his followers. There were many in Canada, including a very famous doctor from Montreal who said that neither of these drugs was dangerous. By fall I had to stop production of that book because the situation had exploded. Originally we had only heard about this from Haight-Ashbury and the east end of New York. At that time there was nothing in Canada. It was not even enough for a footnote in a book.
In September, four months later, I sat with the young who came from eastern Canada, St. Catharines, Durham, Windsor, Hamilton. They were all eastern transients. We called them "hippies". In those days there was only one house of hippies. We called it a crash pad. Within two months every part of the city had these houses filled with circles of pot smokers. In addition, they were mainlining speed. I watched a boy mainline and rush against the wall.
They were joy popping heroin and smoking opium. Two draft dodgers in one house were showing them how to flag. That is shooting a needle in your arm and watching the blood come up.

Maybe you know about it. Maybe you are experts. But the way you talked today I did not think you knew about drugs.
The next thing we knew, they were mainlining chocolate cake, syrup and peanut butter. That was how the needle freak began and heroin started. We saw it all start. Then, as now, in this great and beautiful House members were playing their usual games and not paying attention to what was happening across this country.

Today this subject has been raised in a serious way. It is not political. There is only one member of this House who has made it something political, silly

and immature. I must apologize, Mr. Speaker, for being rude. I have a lot to say, but I guess I had better not.
