subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE GOVERNMENT ACTION TO COMBAT ORGANIZED CRIME
speechtext: The hon. member indicated that in Vancouver drug addiction used to be restricted to about half a block. She put the figure at about 3,300 people. She also indicated that this disease now affects all classes. Does she agree that the reason we are debating this is that this disease now affects the middle class in Canada? One of the reasons we are finally waking up to the problem is that it is affecting our children. We should have been concerned for years about the same problem.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE GOVERNMENT ACTION TO COMBAT ORGANIZED CRIME
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE GOVERNMENT ACTION TO COMBAT ORGANIZED CRIME
speechtext:
I absolutely agree that is true. It is now the children of the professionals and the middle class. That is what has happened. I do not disagree with that.
It was not 3,300 on Vancouver's notorious corner on Hastings Street. There were 2,200 there and 1,100 for the rest of Canada. That is an estimate. I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, but I am not used to speaking from prepared notes and I am sort of lost.
Recently the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) was forced to move by direct indictment in order to get 24 people accused with respect to a drug ring importing from the Golden Triangle, in south east Asia, Laos, Burma and Thailand. There was a mass of undercover work and the arrest of 24 people. As a result drugs in Vancouver have temporarily dried up. Violence has increased. There is not a night goes by without three or four people being attacked. A policeman was shot within the last week. Unfortunately the minister had to move by direct indictment in order to get this case quickly before the courts.
November 12, 1974

Major cases have been delayed in coming before the courts by various stalling techniques. Two and a half years later there is an acquittal because the policemen cannot possibly handle the evidence of years before, mixed with the masses of crime that followed it.
I will simply go on to my recommendations. I have background for them. Mr. Speaker, I think there is a stiffening of public attitude toward drugs and crime. I hope there will be a stiffening here in this House.
We must fill the loopholes that now exist in the Bail Reform Act, but in the meantime we must use the 72 hour holding time which allows the courts to get information. This prevents the release of a drug pusher. If there is evidence of a massive drug operator, and that knowledge is before the courts, I hope bail will be denied. This will entail a speedy trial. I do not believe people should be kept in prison for long periods while the courts play with their cases.
There should be a review of the law on capital punishment to include the mass killers, which are what drug pushers are in our society. I know men are still in prison for life on commuted death sentences for killing one person in a fight; yet we allow these people to go out again on the street and kill thousands and thousands of young people.
I would recommend that we implement, as quickly as possible, Part II of the Narcotics Control Act. It is now on the books, but it has never been implemented. It would require all levels of government to achieve its purposes. It provides for the compulsory treatment of addicts. This is similar to what has happened in Japan and the way they are solving the problem there. But in Japan the addict coming for treatment and returning to drugs, immediately returns to the treatment centre. There is no secret that he must go back if he returns to drugs, and there is no such thing as mere possession. A person who is using drugs today must be a pusher, and there is no conscience among drug users; they will push it on anyone to get their own supplies.
I agree with the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe that there should be preventative correction. It goes back to day one in the life of a child, where there must be intervention to help families who cannot cope with their own problems.
We must find a way to put sanctions on countries like Turkey and those in the Golden Triangle which produce and distribute drugs throughout the world for non-medical use. It is a known fact that social solutions can never keep up with social problems. Perhaps today there was more talk than action, but on serious problems such as we are discussing today this great House of Commons should be seeking answers and solutions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join the others who have congratulated the mover of this motion, not only for bringing this matter to the attention of the House but also for his initial presentation, his reasoned, constructive, philosophical approach to this subject. I should also like to congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs.
Organized Crime
Holt), who has just preceded me. It is obvious to me from the manner in which she presented her case, as well as from my reading of some of the work she has written, that she is perhaps the most knowledgeable person in this area that we have in the House today.
I take it that one of the main roles of parliament is to highlight national problems as revealed to us as members of parliament in our contact with constituents, and in our mail. Organized crime, and law enforcement in connection with organized crime, are certainly one of those problems today. I take it also that the role of the opposition is to criticize from time to time, to propose courses of action, and to suggest alternatives for the government to implement.
I thought I had the parameters of this problem sorted out earlier on this debate until I heard the speech given by the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand). He added another dimension which I find quite terrifying. Not being legally trained I was not aware of the implications of this particular aspect. In this area of international crime I find that the fracturing of responsibility, as mentioned by the minister, is one of the greatest sources of concern. It is one we have overlooked; because of split jurisdictions there is an ever present risk of breakdown in communications, of failure to take action where action is required, and of the danger that we shall fall between two stools or between more than two stools, maybe half a dozen stools, and here we are, flat, to the detriment of society.
We are pleading therefore in this debate for an assertion of positive leadership by the central government in contemplating this international phenomenon, this terrifying spectre. I underline the words "international phenomenon". Only the federal government can act in this area. It must do so.
Two weeks ago I visited all the high schools in my riding. I fondly imagined when I had made arrangements to visit these high schools that I would impart information. It turned out pretty much the other way. I came away with the feeling that I was carrying back with me a good deal more information than I had left behind. One of the most terrifying bits of information I got was connected with drugs. However, from one class-let's be fair-I learned of a community effort in trying to determine whether a pond was being contaminated because of the flow of some polluting material. That was a good community venture.
But in another class, what did I learn? One subject they wanted to talk about was marijuana. "Why don't we legalize it?" they asked. Why don't we make it possible for them to get marijuana? I argued that to do so would be leading further and further into a morass, and that it would lead to heroin. They denied it entirely. "How do you know it will?" they asked. "Have you ever tried it?" "I have never tried it", I told them. "All right, don't talk to us because we have tried it and we know. It does not lead to heroin".
I take the words of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway quite seriously because I know she has studied this seriously, and when she says it leads on, I take it it leads on. I am going to send a copy of these proceedings to that class, not because of my contribution but because of the other contributions which have been made here today.
285.43 - 11

November 12, 1974
Organized Crime
They asked me how I knew it would lead to heroin if I had never tried it. How could I be so positive about it.
The argument continued, and they brought up alcohol and said "Why don't you do something about alcohol?" Well, we all admit alcohol is a problem. I held my ground, but I do not think I persuaded them. I said we were now confronted with a new hallucinogenic compound whose long term effects we did not know, so why broaden the permissive use of this until more is known. We have gone through the alcohol-prohibition kick. We are aware of the evils to which it could give rise, biologically, socially and domestically. We must exercise extreme caution.
Here we have something relatively new on the horizon. Are we going to take those steps which the young want, to legalize even the drug they consider the least harmful, cannabis? I am persuaded that if this is done we will not know the end of that road. We should exercise a good deal more caution regarding drug use than is the case with alcohol when we allocate funds for extensive research, something to which I shall return.
My other reason for urging that there be no extension is in the very nature of the people now using it-people with active, enquiring minds out to experiment. We all did this in our own way at that age, but happily I like to think without such inflammatory materials or quite such dangerous substances. Because of the adventurousness of these youngsters, many may try marijuana and, because the experience seems to give them some sort of a lift, they will try something else, and then they will take more and more. With the ever increasing threshold of tolerance about which we have just heard, they go from cap to cap to many caps, and the problem increases. The social consequences of this course of action are calamitous; we see some evidence of this today.
It is rather interesting to speculate why the roles have changed a little bit on the alcohol-drug scene. These children spoke about the damage that alcohol was doing in their lives. They saw their adult parents in the pubs on Saturday night, then come reeling home while the kids were wondering when supper would be served. The role is now changing: it is the children who are off on a trip and the parents are agonizing where they are, what is going to happen to them and how far they have got mixed up in drugs.
I have also been at meetings where mothers and fathers of drug addicted children pleaded for help. They did not know where to turn. They turn to the police, to social workers and to doctors, but so far there seems to be no real help given these parents, at least not within our present framework. Not enough time or money is devoted to this purpose. Closer municipal, provincial and federal co-operation is required, and I hope the day is not far off when this co-operation will be forthcoming.
There is a court record that appears regularly in either the Colonist or the Times in my area, and 80 per cent of the cases of one particular judge are in the sordid area of drug addiction. Children of 18, 19 and 20 come back to court, and back again. The rulings and endurance of this judge in face of this addiction are stoic in the extreme and he

deserves the maximum support of our community. I hope that the solutions he is looking for will one day emerge.
I maintain that in present day society there has been a breakdown-this was evident from my discussions in the schools-in discipline and self-control within the family, within the schools and within the community. This promotes disrespect for law and for law enforcement. This is a subject that requires much more careful study before we can return to an era when discipline and self-control are qualities that are admirable, not qualities that people can say are of no account.
I am not all that enamoured of statistics, and we have had a good many statistics referred to us tonight showing how many drug addicts there are in Vancouver and in British Columbia in general, and how much it costs to support drug addiction. The figures I have in front of me are official, and show there are 6,500 addicts on the lower mainland, requiring some $350,000 a day to support the habit. I understand more extensive statistics suggest that this figure is closer to 15,000 and that the daily cost is $1 million. These are figures we have heard tonight, but they are worth repeating on the record of today's debate. These aberrations and moral derelictions are supported, promoted, aided and urged on by organized crime, crime that is organized on an international scale.
What can we do, Mr. Speaker, to come to grips with this problem? First of all, 1 suggest we must help the police. We must assist in getting the crime detection duties of our police forces assigned their proper priority, with crime detection itself at the top of the list. Professional training is needed. It has been mentioned before, but I repeat there are other duties now being performed by our police forces which might well be performed by those who are less professionally trained. These lesser duties need to be done, but not at the expense of the high priority that criminal detection requires.
Raids have been carried out, of course, and some of the drugs in use have been picked up; this fact was mentioned by the speaker who immediately preceded me. Rather than cite examples of this, I think some other facts ought to be put on the record. These are to be found in a report already mentioned by a number of speakers, the report by CLEU, initiated by the B.C. government. Federal support was given, but this report was initiated by the B.C. government, for reasons I find difficult to understand; leadership should have come from Ottawa. This report refers to the price spread of these products from when they first arrive until they get on the street. From a price of $7,500 for one pound, purchased direct from the Orient and delivered to Vancouver, the price rises to $22,000 to $25,000 when purchased by the distributor from the importer.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE GOVERNMENT ACTION TO COMBAT ORGANIZED CRIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like many others who have preceded me in this debate today I should like to add my congratulation to the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) on the philosophical manner in which he put the problems, as he terms them in his motion, of "interprovincial crime rings . .. operating out of control in the drug trade in British Columbia, the loan shark business in Ontario and in mafia-type conspiracies in Quebec".
The problems of international and interprovincial crime are, indeed, problems that have occupied the minds of the law makers and law enforcers of this nation and, indeed, of nations throughout the world since the beginning of time. In order to conquer these problems we need fundamental laws. I submit to you that this parliament in the last few years has been passing consistently such laws. We need in addition to good law enforcement-and this requires co-operation at all levels, municipal, provincial and federal, of law enforcement agencies-to ensure that the criminal who dares break the law will meet with the most severe sanctions this parliament can possibly determine.
As is the case with many problems, there are in respect of the drug addict legal problems and medical problems as well. This was pointed out by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt). I feel that in the case of a person who is truly sick, the man who is addicted to the use of this most terrible drug, heroin, and who is at the same time a pusher, he is taking the place of the chain store and the supermarkets on the streets of British Columbia as well as other parts of our nation. It is through that supermarket chain that most people are introduced to the use of heroin. The man who himself must feed his own habit by inducing others to become addicted to drugs is the man who epitomizes the most serious problem we have to face in combating the addiction to drugs, especially heroin, across this nation.
If we go back in the chain of supply we must inevitably come to the commercial trafficker in drugs. Perhaps I might be permitted to call upon my own personal experience in the practice of law in citing a case which illustrates two things; the great benefit which accrues to those who are commercial traffickers in drugs, and the great courage of police officers of this country, as well as of international police forces, in attempting to curb this type of crime.
The particular case I cite took place in this city some few years ago. It involved the co-operation of the United States Bureau of Narcotics and Dangerous Drugs, the RCMP and the Ottawa city police. At the time there was a quantity of heroin of a purity of about 99 per cent being offered for sale. The transaction was to take place in a prominent hotel in this city. I commend the officers involved in this undercover operation for their heroism.
There was one officer in a room with four persons who were trafficking in this drug. The amount involved was valued at some $2.5 million.
He was alone in the room and, as the criminals came in, they frisked him to make sure that he had no weapon on him. His coat was off and a gun was stuck in the small of
28543-11%

November 12, 1974

his back. He was confronted by international elements, one of whom was a French national with a French passport, another a citizen of the United States, and two musclemen who were from the city of Ottawa. They came in to the room with this lone officer who weighed perhaps 150 pounds, a small, defenceless man, by himself, with three and a half kilos of pure heroin. He was there alone to represent the law enforcement agents of this community and in fact all of us.
As the result of good police work international co-operation and good laws in this case, as well as the result of the wiretap which was being taken of the transaction, immediately upon the transaction having been consumat-ed and the illicit substance delivered in the hotel room in Ottawa-the money was delivered simultaneously in another hotel room in New York city, the French national, we believed, having brought the substance to the city- they were all arrested at the same time. As a result of the fact that RCMP officers were in adjacent rooms-I have said there was an undercover operator in the room where the transaction was taking place-and the good work of the Ottawa city policemen-all of whom could have been shot and killed suddenly but this was prevented by better use of detective information-everything ended well.
If I mention that story in order to point out that to combat this type of international crime we in Canada must have effective police work, coupled with good laws, and the best possible technological equipment available to help the police forces.
Let me refer back to the last parliament, the twenty ninth parliament, when, on two separate occasions, the Conservative Party and the NDP joined to vote against the government. On both occasions they produced a catastrophe for themselves and, I believe, for the people of Canada. The last one of those occasions was on July 8 when they voted against us and suffered a loss. The result of that has been a good strong government on this side. But prior to that, and the only other time that the two opposition parties joined their forces to vote against us, was when they wanted to introduce into the protection of privacy act a 90 day warning period, which would mean that 90 days after a wiretap is authorized against someone suspected of having committed a crime he would be notified of it.
Originally the period for which wiretapping was authorized was only 30 days which, in my submission, is far too short a time to allow for any proper detective or investigative work, but in the event that they do not come upon sufficient evidence to lay a charge, at the end of 90 days they would have to notify the person who is under investigation that he has been under electronic surveillance. The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe and the hon. member for New Westminster brought forward that amendment which would have prohibited the type of investigation to which I have referred, which resulted in the apprehension and conviction of international criminals dealing in this most reprehensible of crimes, that is, international trafficking in heroin.
The investigation to which I have referred took many months, many months in the United States and many months in Canada, and the wiretap evidence which was produced at the trial of those individuals was secured by a

court order, not a court order in the province of Ontario or any other jurisdiction within the province, but a court order obtained by the Supreme Court of the State of New York, because that was where the tap was finally put on. There was constant communication between Ottawa and New York while this transaction was taking place.
So it does not make sense for a member of the official opposition to say on one hand that we should do everything we can to combat organized crime-and I agree with that-and on the other hand to speak out of both sides of his mouth and deny agencies what they need in order to investigate and keep under surveillance at all times persons who are engaged in the most reprehensible of all crimes, that is, commercial trafficking in heroin.
The one who is causing us more problems, however, but who could not exist were it not for the former, is the one who is selling four or five caps a day and who is himself an addict and under compulsion, because of his need to feed his habit, to sell to others and, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) said, to induce young children to form this insidious habit. The Narcotic Control Act dates back to 1960 when we were in a different age, a different time. It seems to me that the act needs to be reviewed in its entirety by the government in light of the changing circumstances and changing attitudes of society with respect to the use of drugs. The act has been amended since it was passed in 1960, but not sufficiently.
The riding which I represent has within its boundaries many primary and secondary schools, colleges and universities, and it is of great concern to the people in this community, as it is to the people of British Columbia and all across Canada, that we do what we can, and that we do it as quickly as we can, to point out to the young people- and as a father of five teenagers I am fully aware of the importance of this-that the use of drugs can lead to nothing but harm for them and for those with whom they associate.
The bail reform laws that we have in this country now have had a salutary effect in ensuring that those people who do not have enough money and who were formerly refused bail are now granted their freedom. However, in the prosecution of drug offences it is more the rule than otherwise that a person who is charged with trafficking in heroin is immediately released on bail. And immediately upon his release he will have to go back to his old pattern in order to feed his habit. Such people are often arrested again for the same crime.
I would suggest to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) that the Bail Reform Act should be looked at closely in view of the facts that have emerged since its introduction. Perhaps it should be amended to give precise instructions to the judges who are charged with administering it, rather than the onus being placed on the Crown to demonstrate that the person involved is not likely to show for his trial or that he is likely to commit another crime. We might get to the position where such persons would be kept in custody so long as there was evidence to indicate the likelihood of their committing the same crime again!
I understand that in Vancouver some 3,000 drug cases are awaiting trial. This is because of the Bail Reform Act
November 12, 1974

on the one hand and because of legal aid too, although the latter is a good thing. The same backlog exists in Toronto. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway said a few moments ago, "Justice delayed is justice denied".
I am afraid that during the two years some of those people out on bail are awaiting trial they may commit the same crime again. Unfortunately, even if convicted of the second crime committed while on bail, the sentence is often not as severe as it should be.
If I may comment briefly on the statement of the hon. member for New Westminster, Mr. Speaker, I believe we are dealing with more than just a medical problem when we are dealing with the addict who is also a pusher. This is a very serious social problem which this parliament must face, and perhaps it will be necessary for us to review the Narcotic Control Act in order to deal with it. Traffickers may indeed be sick but they are also committing a criminal offence. There should be strict conditions for parole and medical treatment for such offenders, but not just paper parole and paper medical treatment. There should be effective supervision so that if they dare move into that field again, or induce other persons to use drugs, they would be incarcerated, whether for medical treatment or the protection of society.
Our fundamental problem is how to deter people from engaging in this and indeed all types of criminal activity, and thereby protect society. I heard the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) say that the method of fighting crime in Canada is wrong. Mr. Speaker, my investigations and research indicate that our law enforcement agencies are among the most highly respected in the world. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police is one of the most highly thought of anywhere.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST FOR IMMEDIATE GOVERNMENT ACTION TO COMBAT ORGANIZED CRIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while this country of late has been concerned with the high cost of living and the accompanying economic problems-and so it should-I am pleased that the time has come to bring attention to bear on an area of equally great concern to virtually every Canadian, even if just for a day. I refer, of course, to the ever-growing crime rate and even, in many cases, to the very issue of life and death. The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) should be congratulated for bringing this matter before the House in such an eloquent manner.
The rate of criminal activity is increasing daily in our society and, quite simply, current methods of crime control are obviously not working. We find organized crime making giant inroads into every major city in this country. For example, in Toronto alone, organized crime is
Organized Crime
already well established from the loan sharking field to the narcotics trade. All resources of our police department are being utilized to the maximun and, despite this, we are falling behind in the race even to hold the line on the spread of organized crime in this country.
Of all criminal activities, the most infectious and dangerous is that of the narcotics trade. No one crime so destroys any individual. No one crime is more responsible for over-all criminal activity such as theft, breaking and entering, robbery, prostitution, and crimes of violence within the criminal community itself. For no one crime is it so difficult to convict the ringleaders. No one crime accounts for more police requirements than does this area of activity. Those criminals involved are the worst in our society, for they pick on the weak, the confused, the frustrated and the young, and they spread a disease worse than cancer, a disease that could not only ruin an individual but destroy our whole way of life.
As if this is not enough, we must consider the inroads being made by these traffickers in human misery among our children. Recent reports have indicated an increase in prostitution among 13 and 14 year old girls in an effort to feed their drug habits. In southern Ontario alone the growth of the illegal drug trade has been made painfully obvious by the huge quantities of drugs seized by police authorities. In addition, a number of illegal drug laboratories catering not only to the southern Ontario market but to the export market as well, have been uncovered. It becomes difficult, if not impossible, even to estimate the illicit drug market in this country, but several million dollars each day is not an exaggerated figure.
In spite of all this-in spite of the human misery and the increasing pressure on the police to combat the growth of this illegal drug activity, what do we find the government doing? Mr. Speaker, rather than increasing penalties for importing and trafficking in narcotics and attacking the problem head on, as New York State has done with its tough legislation, the Liberal government sounds out a policy of relaxation on such laws.
I for one would not hesitate to go as far as having trafficking in narcotics included as a capital offence. To touch on capital punishment, Mr. Speaker, when is the government going to have the backbone and guts to enforce the regulations regarding capital punishment already in existence? I refer of course to the killing of policemen and prison guards in the execution of their duty. The time has come to let the criminal element of this country know that the wanton slaying of those who uphold our laws shall be punishable with death. They should pay with their lives. We should set the example, not merely speak about it.
In addition, the parole system which has permitted convicted killers to come out of jail and kill again must no longer be tolerated. Similarly, maximum security institutions to which our hardened criminals have been sentenced must be administered by competent custodians, and not simple minded political hacks who apparently permit these killers to come and go as they please, as witnessed recently at St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary for the third or fourth time in as many years.

November 12, 1974
Organized Crime
Consider this headline in today's Toronto Star, "Escaped killer admits 2 more murders". Arthur Gagnier wrote an "Open Letter to Society", which was published in that newspaper. Gagnier, first convicted of murder at 17, admitted he has killed twice more since he escaped from prison in August. For how long will the government allow this situation to exist? If Gagnier is caught, will the capital punishment provisions of the Criminal Code come into effect? This has not happened in the past, and I doubt if the present government will insist on capital punishment being inflicted in these circumstances.
No killer has the right to inflict his presence on society after he has been sentenced for murder. For if he does, he is living proof that society has no desire to protect itself or protect those hired to protect lives and property. To let him back into society makes a mockery of the law, makes a mockery of those who enacted the legislation, and of those who elected the representatives who passed the legislation.
Another area in which organized crime has made major advances is that of money lending, more commonly known as loan-sharking. In Toronto this practice has led organized criminals to place more and more funds at the disposal of such money lenders. It is estimated that upwards of $100 million is on loan in the cities of Toronto and Montreal. This figure may not be large by itself; but consider the repayment plans. Commonly, 25 per cent is taken off the top of the loan; in addition, between 25 per cent and 50 per cent is charged on the balance each month.
Surely no one is so naive as not to believe the stories of harassment, intimidation and physical injury which result from non-payment. There are many such examples in Toronto alone. Right now an individual in my city is missing and believed dead by the police because of nonrepayment of his loan to loan sharks. It is time for new legislation which will bring these loan sharks to trial. Let us plug loopholes in the Criminal Code and in the Small Loans Act which permit the operations of loan sharks.
Many other areas of crime should come under investigation. For example, to what degree have labour unions been infiltrated by the underworld? To what extent has the laundering of dirty money through legitimate business enterprises been accomplished in this country? To what extent is organized crime manipulating our stock exchanges; and, most important, what can be done to turn the tide in favour of our law enforcement agencies?
Obviously although an increase in manpower would be an asset and greater budgets for technical improvement welcome, such action alone is not enough. Without the legal tools, and without the backing of our courts, we are tying the hands of those very organizations we expect to protect us. Civil liberties organizations demand more and more rights for criminals and are getting them, at the expense of the honest, hard working citizens of this country. They have obtained so much that it has become virtually impossible for police investigation officers to secure convictions in any but the most straightforward and simple cases. In retrospect I, for one, feel that the passage of the wiretapping bill was, in the words of Toronto Police Chief Harold Adamson, "a moment of joy throughout the criminal community". Investigations which might take long months of surveillance if a conviction is to be 
obtained will now be limited to a 90-day period. The hope of conviction in international conspiracies is virtually eliminated.
It is my fervent wish that after this debate we shall see established a government committee which will present new meaningful legislation to equip crime fighting agencies throughout this country with better tools and more power to combat our ever increasing criminal element. Surely the time has come to declare this country's intention to afford safeguards and protection for its citizens.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the mover of the motion, not for what he said in the motion but for the sentiments he expressed. He used to be known as a law and order judge, but in his speech he showed a breadth of sympathy which was refreshing. Let me say this, however: if we were sitting on a jury instead of in the House of Commons, we should be a hung jury. I am glad of the many changes in the law which we introduced in previous parliaments, because they certainly would not be introduced in the present parliament.
Almost everyone who participated in the debate was in favour of capital punishment for all sorts of offences. The last speaker included two or three that had not been mentioned previously. That is not the way to overcome society's difficulties. We, as legislators, must remember that we are not legislating for the present only; we are legislating for future generations. Many ideas expressed today were retrograde rather than progressive.
Little has been said about organized crime in general. An hon. lady spoke about drugs and suggested she knew more than some others about the subject. That may well be so. The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) suggested that we should look at the whole problem and decide how best to solve it. The best way may not be by sending people to jail. God knows, Canada has an unenviable record in sending people to jail. We have the largest jail population, in percentage terms, of any civilized country. If we do what some members suggest, we should need even more jails. Why, we could not even keep up with the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) who seems to think that the solution to our problems is more and bigger penitentiaries.

speechtext:
Yes, squares, one of the reasons is that we have not looked at the Le Dain Report with a view to legalizing or removing marijuana from the penal code.
A few minutes ago a member talked about the RCMP. He stated how wonderful they are. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, they are much like the Ontario Provincial Police who, over the years, have made their reputation tearing up and down the roads on weekends catching people speeding. Previously in this House I mentioned the problem where the RCMP broke into a woman's bathroom. That is what the RCMP, do Mr. Speaker.
What do they accomplish over a weekend? Two or three kids are caught drinking in a pub under age, and one or two kids are caught for personal possession of marijuana. Does that do anything for society? Does it help the situation?
I agree with the hon. member for Saint Hyacinthe. We have to look at the problem and we have to do it in a social sense. In the United States they have said that an addict is not sick. A doctor can no longer prescribe cocaine for his patients.
Great Britain had the same problem. They handled it in a different way. They decided these people could be helped medically. They introduced the registration of addicts, and began to treat them. There are many indications of the results in Great Britain. The crime rate in any major city on the North American continent indicates the results we have had.
Members of parliament should look at this problem in the social sense. For many years they have looked at it in a sense of punishment. That is totally unsatisfactory.
It is not the people on the street who are getting rich. The people who are getting rich are those in organized crime. Even though they are known to the police, they are untouchable. There is not a member of this House who does not know where money can be obtained from one of the crime fields in the drug industry.
Adjournment Debate
We have not attacked this problem. We do not appear to be prepared to attack. I agree with the hon. member for Saint Hyacinthe that it is time wo looked at this problem. What are the social ills being caused by this problem? We must take steps to do something about this.
Policemen in this country are not highly respected. They do jobs that society will not support. Any police force which tries to enforce laws that society does not believe should be retained is not a satisfactory force. It does not have the support of the community.
It is time that we looked at some of the laws which allow organized crime to flourish. We must bring them into line with the thinking of society. Our police forces could then enforce laws that should be enforced. If we do that, we will not have the hang everybody attitude that most members in this debate have talked about. Members will stand up and say they are prepared to look at what society is now, and what the young people are saying. They will consider the most progressive thought possible. We will have legislation that will enable our police forces to operate in a community spirit, enforcing the laws that we make.

EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REPRESENTATION OF PALESTINIANS AT GENEVA CONFERENCE-CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 1 I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) if it was now the opinion of the Canadian government that the Palestinian people should be represented at the Geneva Conference by the PLO. As I indicated in my question, my inquiry was based upon the fact that all the leaders of the Arab states, including His Majesty the King of Jordan, had, at the Rabat summit conference, agreed that the PLO should represent the Palestinian people. My question was also asked against the background of the statement of the Canadian government's point of view expressed by the minister, his predecessor, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), to the effect that the Palestinian people should, in fact, be represented at Geneva.

November 12, 1974
Adjournment Debate
For a long time I had been told that Canada would not prejudge the situation; that the parties involved would decide. I was a little surprised that the minister would reiterate this pat formula after the Rabat conference. If the Canadian government does not agree with the Arab leaders' choice, and apparently it does not or the reply to my question would have been in the affirmative, what group does the government believe should be there? King Hussein has accepted the PLO. Does Canada disagree with him?
I need hardly ask if the government of Canada desires the presence of those splinter Palestinian groups who oppose the PLO for its moderation. Does the government of Canada believe that the Palestinians should appropriately be represented at Geneva by the government of Israel? Putting it simply and directly, it is now a little late to proclaim our unwillingness to prejudge. Judgments of real significance have already been made and we do ourselves and the cause of peace no real good by protective phraseology.
I do not pose questions of this kind to embarrass the minister or the government, for, while I do not have a high regard for the latter, I have the utmost respect and esteem for the former. Rather, am I seeking to stimulate interest in this subject because I verily believe it to be one of the most serious and explosive issues facing the whole of mankind today. The Middle East, the cradle of our civilization, could also be the crucible of its destruction. Through timeless ages this small portion of the globe has heard the clashing of armies and witnessed the crashing of great civilizations. More than once in the last ten years in this House I have recalled fearfully that Armageddon, the prophetic point of no return for mankind, has its locale in the Middle East.
I hope Canada will be strong in the cause of moderation and firm in the exercise of wisdom. We are dealing with an area which has a sad and long record of bad faith, violence, super-power meddling and intense human suffering. It is not helpful now to recall that in the setting up of the state of Israel the U.N. violated one of its fundamental principles-adherence to the right of self-determination.
Nothing is gained, either, by noting that death-dealing raids on Lebanese civilians or Palestinian refugees are no less violent than raids on Israeli citizens within their country. Little is gained by recalling the Arab terrorist acts upon innocent airline passengers while forgetting or condoning the shooting down of a civil Libyan aircraft. Terrorism, violence, threats and intimidation are not the ingredients of settlement.
We must be realistic. It is as unwise as it is immoral to act as though there were no Palestine and no Palestinians. As that brilliant expert on the Middle East, Rabbi Slonim, put it recently: "Only the PLO can be dealt with politically; it is the only representation the Palestinians have. Treating it as though it were not just a monolith of irredeemable terrorists is worth a try."
These and similar counsels of wisdom are worth heeding. Let the Palestinians forsake the threat of some of their numbers to obliterate Israel. It is now a fact of life in

the Middle East. On the other hand, if Israel desires peace-and no part of the region needs it more-let it recognize that its right to existence does not imply existence within borders of its own choosing.
As long ago as 1970, at a meeting of parliamentarians in Cairo, I was presumptuous enough to advise the friends of Palestine as to the unreality of any campaign to erase Israel. At the same time I expressed the view that Israel's borders were not a matter for unilateral decision by that internationally-created entity.
It is my hope that Canada, realistically, patiently and tirelessly, will work toward a day when co-existence will replace terrorism, and violence will give way to enlightened self-interest. I bring to my support a statement by a very great scholar, former President of the Hebrew university in Jerusalem, upon his resignation from the United Jewish Appeal because of its refusal to do anything about the Arab refugees. These are the words of Dr. Juda L. Magnes: "Peace can come only if Israel and Ishmael can feel that they are brothers."

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REPRESENTATION OF PALESTINIANS AT GENEVA CONFERENCE-CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) has made a number of important comments on the situation in the Middle East. His observations in the House are usually witty, perceptive and helpful. I shall certainly not have the time in the few minutes at my disposal to deal with the complex and delicate situation which prevails in the Middle East at the present time, or with the debates which have taken place at the United Nations General Assembly, particularly the debate to commence tomorrow on the Palestinian question.
The hon. gentleman has referred to the question of the representation of the Palestinians at the upcoming Middle East peace negotiations or discussions that will hopefully lead to a peace settlement. We as a government have taken the view that the Palestinian people ought to be represented at any discussions regarding a settlement in the Middle East. It is obvious that the Palestinians constitute an important party to a future settlement and therefore ought to be represented.
When the matter was put before the United Nations, in explaining our abstention we stated that it was not the intention of the Canadian government to prejudge what the form of that representation ought to be. I think this is an appropriate position for Canada to take. We have taken a fair-minded and objective approach to the Middle East situation, and we think we should leave it to the parties themselves to determine what form such representation ought to take.
It is true that at the Rabat summit conference the Arab countries, apparently with the concurrence of the King of Jordan, accepted the PLO as, in their view, the appropriate representative of the Palestinian people. That, of course, is a new factor in the situation.

subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-ALLEGED FAILURE OF POWDERED MILK PROCESSORS AND RETAILERS TO GIVE CONSUMERS BENEFIT OF SUBSIDY-GOVERNMENT ACTION
CONSUMER AFFAIRS-ALLEGED FAILURE OF POWDERED MILK PROCESSORS AND RETAILERS TO GIVE CONSUMERS BENEFIT OF SUBSIDY-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 25 the Food Prices Review Board revealed that during the course of its regular monitoring inspections it found there were instances where the full benefit of the 24 cents per pound subsidy on skim milk powder was not being reflected in retail prices. This discovery was made in a number of stores in Vancouver, Victoria, Winnipeg, Sudbury and Montreal.
The board further indicated that it was not certain whether the retailers or the country's eight skim milk powder processing companies were at fault, and that it had therefore brought the matter to the attention of the agriculture ministry with a request that steps be taken to ensure that all processors and retailers of skim milk powder comply with the spirit and the letter of the subsidy program.
This revelation by the Food Prices Review Board prompted me to ask the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) on October 28 if he would reveal what steps were being taken by his department to recover the money which had been stolen from the public treasury. The minister replied that he would refer my remarks to the Director of Investigation and Research, who would take action in accordance with the provisions of the act. May I point out here that I firmly believe that this action on the part of the retailer or retailers involved was nothing less than fraudulent, nothing less than theft of public funds. We are talking about a government subsidy being paid to stabilize the price of skim milk powder at a reasonable price to the consumer. It is public money, and it belongs back in the pocket of the consumer.
The Retail Council of Canada disagrees with me. Let me quote from the Ottawa Citizen which recorded the remarks of the Retail Council spokesman, Mr. Smith. According to the Citizen he said this:
Stores need not pass on to shoppers the federal subsidy of 24 cents a pound on skim milk powder. The council has advised grocery stores that they are not obliged to give consumers the subsidy. Mr. Smith said retailers have been told they "run the risk of a certain amount of government criticism" if they refuse to pass on the subsidy.
The Citizen went on to say that no law requires the retailers to let government subsidies influence pricing. Mr. Smith then went on to say that retailers have the right to make their own price decisions. That should give Canadians an idea of where the Retail Council stands on the subject of subsidies. What the Retail Council was in effect saying is that they can pocket the money Canadian taxpayers are contributing in an effort to lower the skim milk powder prices. This kind of logic is really ridiculous.
I am 100 per cent positive that not one Canadian consumer wants his tax dollar going into the bulging pockets of the retailers. I should think that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs would have moved on the basis of this statement from the Retail Council. But no, apparently when the Canadian taxpayer provides a subsidy on a product we have to legislate a law that retailers cannot put that subsidy in their pockets.
Adjournment Debate
Let us at this point review the course of action followed by the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. First they embarked on an investigation, presumably to see if the Food Prices Review Board was telling the truth. They found that, and I quote from the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs as reported in Hansard on October 30:
The greater majority of retailers-with only one exception-have passed on the subsidy to consumers.
Apparently the Minister of Agriculture threatened to withdraw the subsidy if the retailer did not comply. I have no argument with that action, but again the logic is ridiculous. However the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs entered into a type of negotiations with the retailer to the effect that: "If you, the retailer, who has been pocketing the taxpayer's money, will now reduce your prices on skim milk powder to an amount equivalent and for a length of time equivalent to that which you overcharged the consumer, then we will not tell the public your name."
Well, for heaven's sake, who does the minister think runs this country? Apparently he does not know, so for his information I should like to point out that taxpayers, the people of Canada, run this country, and they depend upon the minister to make sure their interests are protected. As the minister responsible for consumer affairs he has no darn business protecting the identity of that retailer. I want to know the name of the retailer who was ripping off the Canadian taxpayer and the Canadian consumer, because I do not want to shop there any more, and I bet my constituents do not want to shop there either. I can pick up the newspaper any day and read about the trial of any individual who is accused of wrongdoing. I hope that in his prepared reply the parliamentary secretary to the minister will tell me the name of the retailer who was pocketing the subsidy.
This situation has made it amply clear that the subsidy program as it is presently structured is far too open to ripoffs of the consumer by the retailer. Under its present structure the subsidy is administered by the Department of Agriculture, which pays the subsidy to the processor, who is then responsible for ensuring that the retailer does indeed give the consumer the benefit of such subsidy. If the processor discovers that the subsidy is not being passed on by the retailer, the onus is on the processor to cut off supplies of the subsidized material to the retailer. Then we bave the Food Prices Review Board out watchdogging at public expense, and not having the power even to release the name of the culprit. It is fairly obvious that this Liberal subsidy program does not work for the consumer.
This brings me to my final point, Mr. Speaker. It is absolutely essential that we have a minister of consumer affairs whose purpose is to protect the consumer as he forages for his daily bread in the retail jungle. Indeed, this whole business of the minister being the minister for both consumer and corporate affairs reminds me of the biblical quotation from Matt. 6:24:
No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other.
To paraphrase, Mr. Speaker, the minister cannot serve the consumer and the companies.

speakeroldname: Mr. Norman A. Cafik (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-ALLEGED FAILURE OF POWDERED MILK PROCESSORS AND RETAILERS TO GIVE CONSUMERS BENEFIT OF SUBSIDY-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me first of all state that, as the hon. member is aware, the responsibility for the skim milk subsidy program as such lies with the Department of Agriculture and not with the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
Secondly, as far as the government as a whole is concerned, it is a matter of record that the government not only hoped but fully intended that consumers would receive the full benefit of the subsidy. To this end the Department of Agriculture set up a monitoring program, and through this we know that some outlets have not consistently passed on the subsidy.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) stated in the House on October 28 that his officials have held discussions with the dairy council and the Retail Council of Canada, and have informed non-conforming outlets that the subsidy will be withdrawn from them if it is not fully passed on.
The minister stated, as recorded at page 880 of Hansard for October 30:
The latest report I have had came yesterday. Every retail outlet was passing this saving on to the consumers except for one, and yesterday they thought they would be doing it. I have not received a report on that this morning.
As reported at page 8 of the Globe and Mail of November
5:
A supermarket chain has rolled back a price increase on skim milk powder in face of a Government threat to cut it out of the federal subsidy program. The chain has agreed to lower the price below the regular level by as much as it increased it, and to keep the lower price in effect for as long as it maintained the higher one.
There is no doubt that the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs know and understand the importance of these subsidies being passed on directly to the consumer. The Department of Agriculture has a monitoring program to ensure that that is done, and the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, in the areas where subsidies are under our supervisory control, is doing precisely the same thing.

subtopic: WEIGHTS AND MEASURES-METRIC SYSTEM- COMPENSATION TO SCHOOLS FOR COST OF CONVERSION
WEIGHTS AND MEASURES-METRIC SYSTEM- COMPENSATION TO SCHOOLS FOR COST OF CONVERSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address my comments tonight to the matter of metric conversion. In 1970 parliament endorsed the white paper on metric conversion in Canada, and in June, 1971, the Metric Commission was established by order in council. Its major responsibility, within its terms of reference, was to prepare an over-all plan for conversion to the metric system. This responsibility, which was accepted by the federal government and directly transferred to the commission, is, to my mind, not being fully met by the commission at present, and all the ramifications of that conversion are not apparent to Canadians.
In a recent Gallup poll which was made public on November 2 of this year it was made evident that 62 per cent of Canadians who were questioned on whether or not they understood what the metric system meant said they understood the system. Yet when they were asked to

explain what it was, only 33 per cent related it satisfactorily to the decimal system. It was this minimal knowledge which was regarded as satisfactory so far as the purposes of the poll were concerned.
At present we are faced with the actual conversion to the metric system, and the paramount question with which we are confronted is public education, not only education within our public schools at all levels but the education of the public at large, if the system is to work at all. I believe that the cost of this conversion will be astronomical, and I have not as yet seen anyone come up with a clearcut figure of what the conversion will cost.
However, I should like to point out three areas of which I can think immediately where the costs would have to be substantial. One would be the area of land titles. I believe the old ones will become obsolete because they do not have metric linear measurements. Another is highway signs, which are generally the responsibility of provincial governments. I have seen some changes taking place with regard to present mileage measurements. I believe that conversion will present a major cost. Lastly, we will have conversion in the public education system. A start will have to be made to educate people in the metric system.
We should also consider the cost which will have to be borne by an individual who is, let us say, working as an auto mechanic. He will have to buy another set of tools. Surely the government should give some consideration to a tax writeoff or concession to that individual because of the extra costs he will have to bear.
It is my belief that the federal responsibility with regard to the conversion is based on the fact that the federal government made a decision to convert to the metric system. This was the unanimous decision of the House of Commons, and I accept it. It should also be clear that the federal government has a responsibility in cost sharing for all metric conversion in areas where it has not previously taken financial responsibility because of provincial rights. An example of this is education. The Manitoba Association of School Trustees estimates that the cost of conversion for individuals in the academic stream in schools will be approximately $4 per pupil, and about $50 per pupil in the vocational schools.
If we accept that metric conversion is a federal responsibility then surely it is incumbent upon the government to announce, well in advance of conversion, what form of grants or assistance will be made available to public institutions such as school boards, to cover the costs of conversion. The school boards of Canada get their primary funds from local taxpayers, Mr. Speaker, so I believe it is incumbent upon the government to clarify what steps it will take to east the financial burden of metric conversion on such bodies.

Mr. Speaker, the policy of the government in regard to metric conversion was outlined in the White Paper on Metric Conversion laid before the House in January 1970, and approved by the leaders of all parties. Throughout this White Paper the analysis is based on the assumption that

the costs of conversion will be borne by those incurring them, just as the benefits flowing from conversion will accrue to the individual organization, either directly or through the general health of the economy.
This policy of costs being borne by those incurring them places pressure on the individual organization to apply to the problem of metric conversion, initiative and enterprise to minimize costs. In fact experience in countries such as Great Britain and Australia, which have followed this policy, confirms that conversion in individual firms has generally been achieved at substantially lower costs than were originally estimated.
In the case of education the responsibility for costs is in the jurisdiction of the provinces. Already work done by

the task force of the Council of Ministers of Education indicates that, with imagination, initiative and ingenuity, costs can be kept down. Conversion is being phased in so that some advantage can be taken of obsolescence and the normal patterns of replacement.
